title: The Index-to-Behavior Link: Do FLI Safety Index Scores Predict Subsequent Lab Disclosures?
quick_reasoning: Directly tests whether a safety-governance index changes lab behavior.

original_idea.body:
# The Index-to-Behavior Link: Do FLI Safety Index Scores Predict Subsequent Lab Disclosures?

**Problem:** Reputational-pressure chain: 'index scores a lab low' -> 'public/peer pressure' -> 'lab improves disclosure' -> 'safety practice improves'. The index assumes the score-to-behavior-change link works, but it is untested whether low scores actually move labs toward more disclosure.

**Direction:** Compare FLI AI Safety Index editions over time (Winter 2025, Summer 2025) and code, per indicator and lab, whether a low score in one edition was followed by improved disclosure in the next. Quantify the responsiveness of each safety domain and identify indicators where scoring produced no change, locating where the pressure-to-improvement link fails.

**Why it matters:** If public indices don't change behavior, the field needs binding mechanisms rather than scorecards. Testing the index's own theory of change is high-leverage and only possible with the public editions. No compute, public data, counterfactual and methodologically novel.

**Relevant context:** FLI AI Safety Index Winter 2025 and Summer 2025 editions (33 indicators, 6 domains); Generation Strategy Hint FR67 (apply AI Safety Index methodology to additional dimensions).

title: Redaction as a Broken Link: How Much Safety Information Survives IP-Protection Carve-Outs?
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped measurement of how IP carve-outs gut mandated safety disclosure.

original_idea.body:
# Redaction as a Broken Link: How Much Safety Information Survives IP-Protection Carve-Outs?

**Problem:** Mandated-disclosure chain: 'law requires safety report' -> 'lab publishes report' -> 'report contains decision-relevant detail' -> 'regulator/public can assess'. SB 53 and EU rules let labs redact/summarize to protect IP; the contains-decision-relevant-detail link can be hollowed out by redaction without violating the letter of the law.

**Direction:** Collect the published transparency/system reports issued under emerging disclosure regimes and code each safety-critical claim as fully specified, summarized-away, or redacted. Quantify how much decision-relevant safety content survives the IP carve-out, and identify which claim types are systematically the ones summarized away.

**Why it matters:** Mandatory disclosure only constrains behavior if the disclosure is substantive; showing how IP carve-outs gut the content tells lawmakers exactly which fields need redaction-proof requirements. Public documents, no compute, directly counterfactual.

**Relevant context:** California SB 53 (transparency reports, redaction to protect IP/safety); EU AI Act transparency obligations; arXiv:2512.12443 AI Transparency Atlas (superficial safety disclosures).

title: The Eval-Reproducibility Link: Can an Outsider Reproduce Any Published Dangerous-Capability Claim?
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped reproducibility scorecard for published dangerous-capability evals.

original_idea.body:
# The Eval-Reproducibility Link: Can an Outsider Reproduce Any Published Dangerous-Capability Claim?

**Problem:** Trust-in-evals chain: 'lab runs dangerous-capability eval' -> 'reports a result' -> 'third party can reproduce' -> 'claim is trustworthy'. Third-party auditability is the top open problem; the reproduce link fails when published evals omit prompts, scoring rubrics, or model versions needed to re-run them.

**Direction:** Select a sample of publicly described safety evaluations from system cards and framework appendices and score each on reproducibility prerequisites: is the benchmark named, the prompt set available, the scoring rubric specified, the exact model version identified? Produce a reproducibility scorecard and flag which evals are unauditable in principle.

**Why it matters:** Auditable verification of safety claims is the central technical-governance problem. A concrete catalogue of which published evals can't even in principle be reproduced shows where disclosure standards must require artifacts. Document analysis, no compute, strongly counterfactual.

**Relevant context:** Open Problems in Technical AI Governance (third-party verification, audit consistency); arXiv:2411.13808 'GPAI Evaluations Standards Taskforce'; FLI AI Safety Index risk-assessment domain.

title: Cross-Border Reporting: Where International Incident-Sharing Chains Break at the Border

# Cross-Border Reporting: Where International Incident-Sharing Chains Break at the Border

**Problem:** International-coordination chain: 'incident occurs in country A' -> 'reported to A's authority' -> 'shared with the international network' -> 'other countries adapt'. Establishing consensus evaluation/sharing methods is an open problem; the cross-border-share link likely breaks due to incompatible definitions across national regimes.

**Direction:** Compile the incident/critical-safety-event reporting definitions and thresholds from the major regimes (SB 53, EU AI Act, AISI network statements) and build a compatibility matrix showing where a reportable event in one jurisdiction would not be reportable (or not shareable) in another. Identify the definitional mismatches that break cross-border learning.

**Why it matters:** International consensus on methodology and an NTSB-style learning loop both require compatible definitions. A mismatch matrix tells coordinators exactly which definitional gaps block cross-border safety learning. Pure comparative policy analysis, no compute, high counterfactual value.

**Relevant context:** arXiv:2511.05914 incident reporting institutional design; SB 53 critical safety incident reporting; EU AI Office notification; International Network of AI Safety Institutes.

title: Agent Sandbox Escape: Prototyping the Containment Link in the Autonomous-Misuse Chain

original_idea.body:
# Agent Sandbox Escape: Prototyping the Containment Link in the Autonomous-Misuse Chain

**Problem:** Agentic-misuse chain: 'agent given a task' -> 'agent takes actions via tools' -> 'sandbox contains side effects' -> 'no real-world harm'. As governance shifts to autonomous agents, the containment link is under-specified; few beginner-accessible artifacts show how easily a tool-using agent exceeds its intended scope.

**Direction:** Build a minimal monitoring harness around a small open model acting as a tool-using agent in a constrained sandbox (file + shell tools), and log every action against an allowlist policy. Measure how often the agent attempts out-of-policy actions on benign tasks and which simple policy rules catch them. Ship the harness as reusable safety infrastructure.

**Why it matters:** Strategically valuable monitoring/sandbox infrastructure is exactly the kind of counterfactual work labs deprioritize. A small open prototype that quantifies containment-link failures and is reusable by others advances agent governance concretely. Small open model, one GPU, no training.

**Relevant context:** microsoft/agent-governance-toolkit (policy enforcement, execution sandboxing, OWASP Agentic Top 10); arXiv:2505.18003 'An Example Safety Case for Safeguards Against Misuse'; structured access literature.

title: The Self-Assessment Link: Comparing Lab Self-Reports Against Independent FLI Scores

# The Self-Assessment Link: Comparing Lab Self-Reports Against Independent FLI Scores

**Problem:** Assurance chain: 'lab self-reports safety practice' -> 'self-report taken at face value' -> 'stakeholders trust it'. The FLI Index moved deliberately from self-reporting to publicly-verifiable evidence; this implies the self-report-to-truth link is unreliable, but the size of the gap is undocumented per indicator.

**Direction:** For indicators where both a lab self-description and an independent FLI panel score exist, code the discrepancy: does the lab claim a practice the panel found unsubstantiated? Quantify, per safety domain, how often self-reports overstate relative to evidence-based scoring, locating where self-assessment most diverges from verifiable reality.

**Why it matters:** Much governance still relies on self-reporting; measuring the self-report-vs-evidence gap by domain tells regulators where independent verification is non-negotiable. Uses only public Index materials and lab statements, no compute, counterfactual.

**Relevant context:** FLI AI Safety Index Summer 2025 (shift from self-reporting to publicly verifiable evidence, 33 indicators); arXiv:2512.01166 'Evaluating AI Companies' Frontier Safety Frameworks'.

title: Benchmark-to-Threshold: Does Any Public Eval Actually Map to a Framework Capability Threshold?

# Benchmark-to-Threshold: Does Any Public Eval Actually Map to a Framework Capability Threshold?

**Problem:** Threshold-grounding chain: 'framework defines a capability threshold' -> 'a concrete benchmark operationalizes it' -> 'a score crosses the threshold' -> 'action triggered'. The benchmark-operationalizes link is frequently missing: thresholds are described qualitatively with no named, runnable benchmark.

**Direction:** Enumerate every capability threshold across public frameworks (RSP, Preparedness, FSF) and attempt to match each to a specific named, publicly available benchmark that could operationalize it. Quantify the fraction of thresholds with no public benchmark anchor, and characterize which risk areas (e.g., AI R&D self-improvement) are most un-operationalized.

**Why it matters:** A threshold with no measurable benchmark can never fire. Showing which thresholds float free of any benchmark tells the evaluation-standards community where to build missing benchmarks. Document mapping, lightweight benchmark survey, no compute, counterfactual.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic RSP (CBRN, AI R&D thresholds); OpenAI Preparedness (Bio, Cyber, Autonomous Replication, Self-Improvement); DeepMind FSF Critical Capability Levels; arXiv:2411.13808 GPAI Evaluations Standards Taskforce.

title: The Safety-Buffer Link: Are Stated Buffers Large Enough to Catch Capability Jumps?
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped check of whether re-eval safety buffers absorb realistic capability jumps.

original_idea.body:
# The Safety-Buffer Link: Are Stated Buffers Large Enough to Catch Capability Jumps?

**Problem:** Early-warning chain: 'evaluate at compute interval' -> 'safety buffer absorbs capability jump since last eval' -> 'threshold caught before crossed in deployment'. Frameworks set re-eval cadences (e.g., DeepMind every 6x compute) and 'safety buffers', but whether the buffer-vs-jump link holds given known capability scaling is unexamined publicly.

**Direction:** Using public scaling-trend data (e.g., benchmark gains per compute multiple from open leaderboards), estimate how much capability can plausibly increase within one stated re-evaluation interval, and compare to the stated safety buffer. Identify cadences where a single inter-eval jump could plausibly leap past a threshold undetected.

**Why it matters:** Safety buffers are the mechanism meant to prevent surprise threshold-crossings; a back-of-envelope check of whether buffers exceed realistic jumps tells labs/regulators whether re-eval cadence is too coarse. Uses only public benchmark/scaling data, light statistics, no compute, counterfactual.

**Relevant context:** DeepMind FSF (re-eval every 6x compute / 3 months fine-tuning); Anthropic RSP safety buffers; Epoch AI compute/benchmark tracking data (subfield Key Datasets).

title: Definitional Divergence: Tracing Where 'Frontier Model' Scope Filters Out Real Risk
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped mapping of regulatory scope exclusions that leave risky models ungoverned.

original_idea.body:
# Definitional Divergence: Tracing Where 'Frontier Model' Scope Filters Out Real Risk

**Problem:** Scope chain: 'risky model exists' -> 'it falls within the regulated definition' -> 'obligations attach' -> 'risk governed'. The falls-within-definition link breaks when FLOP-based or revenue-based thresholds (10^25 EU, 10^26 US, SB 53 criteria) exclude genuinely risky models, leaving them ungoverned.

**Direction:** Compile the scoping criteria of the major regimes (EU AI Act, SB 53, US reporting) and build a decision tree, then test it against a list of known/announced models and capability-eliciting techniques (fine-tunes, agent scaffolds) to find risky configurations that fall outside every definition. Catalogue the systematic exclusions.

**Why it matters:** If the regulatory definition misses real risk, all downstream obligations never attach. Mapping the exclusion zone tells legislators where definitions must shift from compute-only to capability-based scoping. Pure policy analysis, no compute, strongly counterfactual.

**Relevant context:** EU AI Act 10^25 FLOP systemic-risk threshold; US 10^26 reporting threshold; SB 53 frontier-model criteria; arXiv:2505.17109 open-weight policy gaps.

title: The Pause-Button Link: Stress-Testing Whether Compute Governance Could Actually Halt Training
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses feasibility of compute-governance emergency halt, a long-horizon safety lever.

original_idea.body:
# The Pause-Button Link: Stress-Testing Whether Compute Governance Could Actually Halt Training

**Problem:** Emergency-halt chain: 'dangerous run detected' -> 'authority issues halt' -> 'compute is actually stopped' -> 'training ceases'. Proposals describe compute governance as a 'pause button', but the issue-to-actually-stopped link assumes enforceable control over distributed, fungible compute, which is undemonstrated.

**Direction:** From the compute-governance literature, decompose the proposed pause mechanism into required preconditions (chip registry, location attestation, kill-switch authority, jurisdiction) and assess, with public evidence, which preconditions currently exist versus are aspirational. Produce a readiness scorecard for the pause-button chain and flag the single weakest precondition.

**Why it matters:** Compute governance is a leading lever for medium/long-horizon catastrophic risk that frontier labs won't build; a clear-eyed audit of which pause-button preconditions are real tells the field where to invest. Pure literature synthesis, no compute, very counterfactual and long-horizon.

**Relevant context:** arXiv:2506.20530 'Toward a Global Regime for Compute Governance: Building the Pause Button'; arXiv:2604.04712 hardware-level governance feasibility taxonomy; LessWrong compute governance literature review.

title: The Source-Credibility Link: How Often Do Safety-Framework Claims Rest on Non-Peer-Reviewed Evidence?
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses the evidentiary basis and auditability of safety claims.

original_idea.body:
# The Source-Credibility Link: How Often Do Safety-Framework Claims Rest on Non-Peer-Reviewed Evidence?

**Problem:** Evidence-quality chain: 'lab asserts a safety property' -> 'assertion is backed by credible evidence' -> 'stakeholders can rely on it'. The backed-by-credible-evidence link weakens when frameworks cite internal blog posts or unpublished results rather than peer-reviewed or reproducible work.

**Direction:** Audit the citations/evidence basis of safety claims in public frameworks and system cards, classifying each supporting source by credibility tier (peer-reviewed / credible preprint / internal-unpublished / blog). Quantify what fraction of safety-critical claims rest only on non-verifiable internal sources, locating where the evidence chain is weakest.

**Why it matters:** Whether safety claims are auditable depends on their evidentiary basis; showing how many rest on uncheckable internal sources motivates standards requiring reproducible evidence. Document analysis, no compute, counterfactual, and directly aligned with source-credibility evaluation norms.

**Relevant context:** Open Problems in Technical AI Governance (third-party auditability); arXiv:2512.01166 evaluating frontier safety frameworks; FLI AI Safety Index (publicly verifiable evidence basis); CLAUDE.md source-credibility criteria.

title: Backcasting from 'Every System Card Is Machine-Readable': A Cross-Lab Disclosure Completeness Audit
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped cross-lab safety-disclosure completeness scorecard.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting from 'Every System Card Is Machine-Readable': A Cross-Lab Disclosure Completeness Audit

**Problem:** A safety success state where third parties can automatically audit frontier safety claims requires standardized, comparable disclosures. Today system/model cards from different labs use wildly inconsistent structures (one study found 947 unique section names across frontier and Hugging Face cards), so no automated cross-lab comparison is possible.

**Direction:** Collect the publicly available system/model cards for ~8-12 frontier models (Claude, GPT, Gemini, Llama, Grok, DeepSeek, etc.), define a fixed checklist of safety-critical disclosure items (dangerous-capability eval results, elicitation methodology, third-party access, refusal/jailbreak testing, training-data provenance), then hand-code each card for presence/absence/depth using a simple rubric. Quantify completeness gaps and section-naming variance. Optionally use an LLM with a fixed prompt to extract fields and validate against the hand-coding.

**Why it matters:** Backcasting from 'auditable safety claims' shows the missing precondition is comparable disclosure. A concrete completeness scorecard reveals exactly which safety items labs omit, giving regulators and the AI Safety Index a reproducible gap map. No model training, no proprietary data — pure public-document analysis that an outsider can do better than a lab.

**Relevant context:** AI Transparency Atlas (arXiv:2512.12443) found 947 unique section names and proposed a weighted 8-section framework. FLI AI Safety Index scores 33 indicators on publicly verifiable evidence. Open Problems in Technical AI Governance (arXiv:2407.14981) lists verification as a core capacity.

title: Backcasting from 'Safety Frameworks Are Enforceable': Quantifying Vagueness in Responsible Scaling Policies
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped enforceability index for responsible scaling policy commitments.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting from 'Safety Frameworks Are Enforceable': Quantifying Vagueness in Responsible Scaling Policies

**Problem:** A success state where voluntary frontier safety frameworks become enforceable requires that their commitments be specific enough to verify. Today many commitments are vague ('we will evaluate for dangerous capabilities') with no measurable trigger, so the gap between voluntary codes and enforceable standards persists.

**Direction:** Assemble the published safety frameworks (Anthropic RSP, OpenAI Preparedness, Google DeepMind FSF, Meta, xAI, etc.), then build a rubric scoring each commitment sentence on specificity: is there a quantitative threshold? a named evaluation? a defined responsible party? a deadline? a consequence for breach? Use simple text classification (manual + an LLM second-pass with a fixed rubric) to score every commitment and produce a per-lab 'enforceability index'.

**Why it matters:** Working backward from enforceability shows the precondition is operationalized, testable commitments. A vagueness/specificity score makes the EU AI Office's exact problem (voluntary vs enforceable gap) measurable and tells regulators which clauses need tightening. Counterfactually strong: outsiders are better positioned to grade vagueness than the labs writing the documents.

**Relevant context:** A Grading Rubric for AI Safety Frameworks (arXiv:2409.08751); 16 companies made Frontier AI Safety Commitments (May 2024); EU GPAI Code of Practice bridges the voluntary-standards gap. Open Problems in Technical AI Governance emphasizes operationalization.

title: Backcasting from 'No Eval Is Defeated by Trivial Prompt Changes': Measuring Prompt-Sensitivity of a Public Dangerous-Capability Benchmark
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped measurement of elicitation-induced variance in dangerous-capability evals.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting from 'No Eval Is Defeated by Trivial Prompt Changes': Measuring Prompt-Sensitivity of a Public Dangerous-Capability Benchmark

**Problem:** A success state where dangerous-capability evaluations reliably inform deployment decisions requires that scores not swing wildly with elicitation tweaks. Research shows small elicitation improvements dramatically raise scores, meaning naive evals under-report risk — undermining any governance regime built on them.

**Direction:** Take one open dangerous-capability-adjacent benchmark (e.g., a bio/cyber-knowledge MCQA set or WMDP-style public subset) and a small open model on a single GPU. Run the benchmark under N controlled prompt variations (formatting, few-shot, role framing, chain-of-thought on/off) and measure score variance. Report how much 'measured capability' moves purely from elicitation, with statistics on which perturbations matter most.

**Why it matters:** Backcasting from 'governance can trust eval numbers' exposes elicitation-induced variance as the missing reliability precondition. Demonstrating that a governance-relevant score is fragile to prompt choice is a concrete warning for International Network of AI Safety Institutes consensus efforts. Needs only a small open model and public benchmark — ideal outsider work.

**Relevant context:** FLI Summer 2025: naive elicitation causes under-reporting; only 3/7 labs test dangerous capabilities. 'How Should AI Safety Benchmarks Benchmark Safety?' (arXiv:2601.23112) stresses prompt versioning and reproducibility. International Network of AI Safety Institutes seeks eval consensus.

title: Backcasting from 'A Working National AI Incident Reporting System': Mapping Coverage Gaps in the Existing Incident Database
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses coverage gaps in AI incident data for an incident-response regime.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting from 'A Working National AI Incident Reporting System': Mapping Coverage Gaps in the Existing Incident Database

**Problem:** A success state with an NTSB-style national AI incident response capability requires comprehensive, well-classified incident data. Today incident reporting is fragmented across databases with inconsistent taxonomies, so we cannot tell which harm categories are systematically under-reported.

**Direction:** Download the public AI Incident Database (AIID) export and classify a sample of incidents against the CSET AI Harm Taxonomy and MIT AI Risk Repository categories using a fixed rubric (manual + LLM-assisted). Analyze the distribution: which sectors, harm types, and severities dominate; which are absent; how reporting lag and source type bias the record. Output a coverage-gap report that a hypothetical incident-response body would need.

**Why it matters:** Backcasting from 'effective incident response' shows the precondition is unbiased, complete incident data. Quantifying systematic blind spots tells policymakers where mandatory reporting would add most value. Pure public-data analysis, no lab resources, directly serving The Future Society's NTSB-analogue agenda.

**Relevant context:** AIID and AIAAIC databases; CSET AI Harm Taxonomy; MIT AI Risk Repository; Stanford HAI 2025 found incidents up 56.4% in 2024. 'Scalable AI Incident Classification' (incidentdatabase.ai) used LLM classification against MIT taxonomies.

title: Backcasting from 'Compute Thresholds Track Real Risk': Stress-Testing the 1e25 FLOP Systemic-Risk Trigger
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped analysis of FLOP-to-capability drift undermining systemic-risk thresholds.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting from 'Compute Thresholds Track Real Risk': Stress-Testing the 1e25 FLOP Systemic-Risk Trigger

**Problem:** A success state where compute thresholds (e.g., EU AI Act's 1e25 FLOP) correctly identify systemic-risk models requires that the threshold correlate with actual dangerous capability. With efficiency gains (~40%/year more compute-per-dollar), a fixed FLOP line may misclassify models, letting capable-but-efficient models slip below it.

**Direction:** Using Epoch AI's public model database (3200+ models with compute estimates) plus public benchmark scores (e.g., MMLU/GPQA leaderboards), build a simple regression/scatter analysis of training-FLOP vs measured capability over time. Quantify how the FLOP-to-capability mapping drifts with algorithmic efficiency, and estimate how many models cross capability bars while sitting below 1e25 FLOP. Produce a 'threshold drift' visualization.

**Why it matters:** Backcasting from 'thresholds gate the right models' reveals the precondition that compute must proxy capability stably — which efficiency progress erodes. A concrete drift analysis warns regulators that static FLOP thresholds decay, informing compute-governance design. Uses only Epoch's open data; no training, strong outsider counterfactual.

**Relevant context:** Epoch AI: frontier compute grows 4-5x/yr, compute-per-dollar +40%/yr; EU AI Act systemic-risk threshold = 1e25 FLOP. Open Problems in Technical AI Governance treats compute as a blunt but key lever; Lennart Heim's compute-governance work.

title: Backcasting from 'Outsiders Can Verify a Model's Identity': A Lightweight Model-Fingerprinting Probe
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped model-identity verification probe for third-party safety auditing.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting from 'Outsiders Can Verify a Model's Identity': A Lightweight Model-Fingerprinting Probe

**Problem:** A success state for third-party verification requires being able to confirm that a deployed API actually serves the model a lab claims (no silent swap to a cheaper/less-safe model). Today external auditors have no cheap way to verify model identity behind an API.

**Direction:** On open models accessible via API or local hosting, build a small behavioral 'fingerprint' — a fixed battery of low-temperature prompts whose answer patterns are model-specific — and test whether you can distinguish models (e.g., two Llama variants, a base vs fine-tuned version) reliably above chance. Quantify how many probe queries are needed and how robust the fingerprint is to sampling settings.

**Why it matters:** Backcasting from 'verifiable deployment claims' shows the precondition is cheap external model-identity verification. A working fingerprinting prototype gives regulators and auditors a tool to detect undisclosed model swaps. Needs only API/local access to open models — exactly the structured-access verification gap outsiders can prototype.

**Relevant context:** Open Problems in Technical AI Governance lists verification/access as core capacities; 'Toward Trustworthy AI Development' (arXiv:2004.07213) on verifiable claims; Laminator (arXiv:2406.17548) on verifiable ML property cards via attestation.

title: Backcasting from 'Security vs Innovation Framing Doesn't Hide Capitulation': Content-Analyzing AISI/CAISI Communications
quick_reasoning: Relevant to international safety coordination but link to a safety outcome is somewhat indirect.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting from 'Security vs Innovation Framing Doesn't Hide Capitulation': Content-Analyzing AISI/CAISI Communications

**Problem:** A success state where national AI institutes coordinate effectively requires understanding whether divergent framings (UK 'AI Security Institute' vs US 'CAISI' innovation framing) reflect real policy divergence or just branding. We lack a systematic comparison of what these bodies actually prioritize.

**Direction:** Collect public documents from UK AISI, US CAISI/NIST, and 2-3 other national institutes (blog posts, frameworks, eval reports). Build a coded content analysis: frequency of safety vs capability vs economic terms, topics evaluated, binding vs voluntary language. Use simple NLP (keyword/topic counts, sentiment, an LLM-coded topic taxonomy with a fixed rubric) to quantify framing divergence and overlap.

**Why it matters:** Backcasting from 'effective international coordination' shows the precondition is shared substantive priorities, not just shared labels. Quantifying whether 'security vs innovation' is rhetoric or real divergence directly follows up the surprising AISI/CAISI renaming result and informs the International Network of AI Safety Institutes. Public-document analysis, no lab access needed.

**Relevant context:** Subfield surprising result: UK AISI renamed 'AI Security Institute', US AISI renamed CAISI (innovation framing). International Network of AI Safety Institutes; MIRI 2025 governance agenda on strategic landscape.

title: Backcasting from 'Open-Weight Release Decisions Are Evidence-Based': A Reproducible Marginal-Risk Mini-Audit
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped marginal-risk uplift audit operationalizing open-weight release decisions.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting from 'Open-Weight Release Decisions Are Evidence-Based': A Reproducible Marginal-Risk Mini-Audit

**Problem:** A success state for open-weight governance requires release decisions grounded in measured marginal risk (what new capability does releasing this model add beyond already-available models?). Today this marginal analysis is rarely done quantitatively, so 'marginal risk is low' is asserted, not shown.

**Direction:** Pick a dual-use-adjacent but safe public benchmark (e.g., a hazardous-knowledge MCQA proxy or a public cyber-CTF reasoning set) and compare a newly-released open model against an older open model and a closed API on that benchmark, computing the marginal score delta. Demonstrate a small, reproducible 'marginal capability uplift' workflow that a release-decision body could run, with explicit success criteria and uncertainty bounds.

**Why it matters:** Backcasting from 'sound open-weight release decisions' shows the missing precondition is a cheap, standardized marginal-uplift measurement. A reproducible mini-audit operationalizes the OECD marginal-risk concept into something a small actor can run. No training, only inference on public/open models — high counterfactual value for a medium-horizon proliferation threat.

**Relevant context:** OECD.AI marginal-risk analysis for open-weight models; 'Estimating Worst-Case Frontier Risks of Open-Weight LLMs' (arXiv:2508.03153); International AI Safety Report 2026. Open Problems in Technical AI Governance on operationalization.

title: Backcasting from 'AI Safety Index Scores Are Robust': A Sensitivity Analysis of the Index Methodology
quick_reasoning: Directly tests robustness of a key safety-governance benchmark methodology.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting from 'AI Safety Index Scores Are Robust': A Sensitivity Analysis of the Index Methodology

**Problem:** A success state where the FLI AI Safety Index meaningfully pressures labs requires that its grades be robust to reasonable methodology choices. With 33 indicators across 6 domains aggregated into letter grades, the final ranking may be sensitive to weighting and aggregation decisions that aren't transparently justified.

**Direction:** Reconstruct the AI Safety Index's published per-indicator scores for the labs, then re-run the aggregation under alternative weightings (equal weights, safety-domain-heavy, dropping low-evidence indicators) and alternative aggregation rules (mean vs min vs rank). Measure how much lab rankings change. Produce a robustness/sensitivity report identifying which grades are stable and which are artifacts of methodology.

**Why it matters:** Backcasting from 'the Index is a trustworthy governance signal' shows robustness-to-methodology as the precondition. The strategy hints explicitly suggest varying the AI Safety Index methodology. A sensitivity analysis strengthens (or appropriately tempers) the Index's influence. Pure public-data reanalysis — exactly the FR67 'apply to additional dimensions' suggestion.

**Relevant context:** FLI AI Safety Index Summer/Winter 2025: 33 indicators, 6 domains, no lab above C+. Strategy hint FR67 explicitly names 'AI Safety Index methodology (apply to additional dimensions)'. 'Evaluating AI Companies' Frontier Safety Frameworks' (arXiv:2512.01166).

title: Backcasting from 'Eval Results Are Comparable Across Institutes': Reproducing One Eval Two Ways
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped reproducibility test of eval implementations for cross-institute recognition.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting from 'Eval Results Are Comparable Across Institutes': Reproducing One Eval Two Ways

**Problem:** A success state where international AI safety institutes can mutually recognize each other's evaluations requires that the same eval yield comparable results across implementations. Tiny differences in scaffolding, scoring, and prompts can make 'the same benchmark' produce divergent numbers, blocking mutual recognition.

**Direction:** Take one public safety/capability eval with an available reference implementation, then independently re-implement its scoring/scaffolding from the paper description and run both on the same small open model. Quantify the gap between the reference and the independent re-implementation, and isolate which under-specified choices (parsing, scoring tolerance, prompt template) drive divergence.

**Why it matters:** Backcasting from 'cross-institute mutual recognition' shows implementation-reproducibility as the precondition. Demonstrating how much a faithful re-implementation diverges is a concrete argument for stricter eval specification standards in the International Network of AI Safety Institutes. Needs one small open model and public eval code — clean outsider experiment.

**Relevant context:** International Network of AI Safety Institutes seeks shared eval methodology; 'How Should AI Safety Benchmarks Benchmark Safety?' (arXiv:2601.23112) on verbatim versioning of prompts/rubrics; Inspect/lm-eval-harness ecosystems for reference implementations.

title: Backcasting from 'Frontier Commitments Are Kept': A Longitudinal Commitment-Tracking Diff
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses detecting silent weakening of voluntary safety commitments.

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting from 'Frontier Commitments Are Kept': A Longitudinal Commitment-Tracking Diff

**Problem:** A success state where voluntary commitments mean something requires the ability to detect when labs quietly weaken or drop them. Frameworks are revised over time, and there is no easy public view of how a lab's commitments have changed version-to-version.

**Direction:** Use the public version history (Wayback Machine / archived PDFs) of 2-3 labs' safety frameworks and produce a structured diff: which commitments were added, softened, removed, or had thresholds changed between versions. Classify each change as strengthening/weakening using a fixed rubric. Build a simple timeline visualization of commitment drift per lab.

**Why it matters:** Backcasting from 'commitments are durable' shows change-detection as the precondition for accountability. A version-diff catches silent walk-backs that single-snapshot scorecards miss, complementing AI Lab Watch and the AI Safety Index. Entirely public-document work that outsiders are well-placed to do as a watchdog function.

**Problem:** Failure mode A: chip export rules use per-transaction quantity thresholds (e.g. ~1,700 H100-equivalents without a license). Failure mode B: compute tracking is weak at aggregating across many small purchasers. Together, an adversary stays under the per-purchase threshold while aggregating cluster-scale compute the licensing regime was meant to catch.

**Direction:** Build a small agent-based / Monte-Carlo simulation of buyers making repeated just-under-threshold purchases through shell intermediaries, and measure how much aggregate compute can be assembled before any single rule fires, under different threshold and aggregation-window settings. Sweep policy parameters to find which combinations close the loophole.

**Why it matters:** Turns an anecdotal smuggling loophole into a quantified policy-parameter map regulators can use to set thresholds and aggregation windows. Simulation only — no hardware, no proprietary data, ideal beginner project with clear success criteria.

**Relevant context:** Tier-2 ~1,700-chip loophole and circumvention reporting (techpolicy.press; aei.org); Toward a Global Regime for Compute Governance (arXiv:2506.20530).

# Eval Saturation x Risk Tiering: When Maxed-Out Benchmarks Stop Differentiating Dangerous Models

**Problem:** Failure mode A: capability benchmarks saturate (top models all near ceiling). Failure mode B: governance risk tiers rely on benchmark scores to separate 'systemic-risk' from ordinary models. When the benchmark saturates, the tiering signal collapses — two very differently dangerous models look identical, so mitigation obligations are mis-assigned.

**Direction:** Take a public safety/capability benchmark and several open models of varying size. Show empirically where scores compress at the top, then quantify how much discriminative power (e.g. score variance / rank separability) the benchmark loses as models improve. Translate the loss-of-separation into 'how confidently could a regulator tier these models?' Provide a saturation-monitoring metric.

**Why it matters:** Demonstrates that the metric backbone of risk-tiered governance degrades exactly as capabilities (and stakes) rise. Cheap, public-model analysis; directly informs international eval-methodology standards work.

**Relevant context:** Open Problems in Technical AI Governance on assessment limits (arXiv:2407.14981); International Network of AI Safety Institutes consensus goal (FLI AI Safety Index).

title: API-Access Restrictions x Third-Party Audit Mandates: The Accountability Paradox Quantified

original_idea.body:
# API-Access Restrictions x Third-Party Audit Mandates: The Accountability Paradox Quantified

**Problem:** Failure mode A: governance increasingly mandates independent third-party audits. Failure mode B: providers tighten API/logprob/system-access restrictions. The two collide: the audits regulators require become technically impossible to perform, so 'audited' becomes a paper formality.

**Direction:** Catalogue the access surfaces (logprobs, system prompts, fine-tuning, rate limits, ToS audit clauses) actually offered by ~6 major public APIs, then map each against the concrete data access that a published audit method (e.g. a red-team or bias audit) requires. Produce an 'auditability matrix' showing which mandated audits are currently un-runnable, and which API change would unlock each.

**Why it matters:** Operationalizes the documented accountability paradox into a checklist regulators can attach to audit mandates. Needs only public API docs and ToS — quintessential civil-society work labs won't do against themselves.

**Relevant context:** The Accountability Paradox / platform API restrictions (arXiv:2505.11577); third-party audit access roadblocks (ccgnludelhi.wordpress.com); EU AI Act conformity assessments.

title: Voluntary-Commitment Drift x No-Versioning: Tracking Silent Walk-Backs in Frontier Safety Policies

original_idea.body:
# Voluntary-Commitment Drift x No-Versioning: Tracking Silent Walk-Backs in Frontier Safety Policies

**Problem:** Failure mode A: safety commitments are voluntary and editable. Failure mode B: there is no canonical version history, so weakened wording is invisible. Together, a lab can quietly relax a commitment (e.g. raising a capability threshold) with no governance signal — a compound erosion of accountability.

**Direction:** Use the Wayback Machine and METR's 'Common Elements' framework to diff successive versions of 4-6 labs' published frontier-safety/responsible-scaling policies over time. Code each change as strengthening/weakening/neutral against a fixed rubric, and chart the net drift. Surface specific silent walk-backs with before/after quotes.

**Why it matters:** Creates a reproducible commitment-drift monitor — the kind of independent watchdog infrastructure the ecosystem lacks. Purely archival + light NLP; high counterfactual value and a strong blog narrative.

**Relevant context:** METR Common Elements of Frontier AI Safety Policies (metr.org/common-elements); MIRI governance agenda on enforceability gaps (intelligence.org 2025).

title: Refusal Brittleness x Jailbreak Disclosure Lag: How a Capability Eval and an Incident Channel Both Miss the Same Harm
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped study of the blind window between refusal certification and incident reporting.

original_idea.body:
# Refusal Brittleness x Jailbreak Disclosure Lag: How a Capability Eval and an Incident Channel Both Miss the Same Harm

**Problem:** Failure mode A: pre-deployment refusal evals certify a model 'safe' on harmful prompts. Failure mode B: incident/jailbreak reporting is slow and voluntary, so post-deployment failures aren't logged. A jailbreak that defeats the certified refusal lands in the gap between the two systems and is governed by neither.

**Direction:** On an open model, take a sample of harmful prompts it refuses (passing a mock 'eval'), apply a handful of well-known public jailbreak templates, and measure the refusal-collapse rate. Then estimate the reporting lag: search the AI Incident Database / public trackers for how long analogous jailbreaks took to be logged. Quantify the combined 'certified-but-broken-and-unreported' exposure window.

**Why it matters:** Shows that static refusal certification plus laggy incident reporting jointly leave a structural blind window, motivating mandatory post-deployment monitoring. No training; uses public jailbreak templates and one open model.

**Relevant context:** Incident reporting underreporting (arXiv:2511.05914); refusal removal/jailbreak literature; Open Problems in Technical AI Governance assessment gaps (arXiv:2407.14981).

title: Security-vs-Innovation National Framing x Eval Non-Harmonization: Simulating Coordination Breakdown
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses jurisdiction-shopping risk from non-harmonized safety evals.

original_idea.body:
# Security-vs-Innovation National Framing x Eval Non-Harmonization: Simulating Coordination Breakdown

**Problem:** Failure mode A: national institutes adopt divergent framings (UK 'AI Security Institute' vs US 'CAISI' innovation framing), implying different eval priorities. Failure mode B: there is no harmonized eval methodology. Together, the same model can pass one nation's bar and fail another's, enabling jurisdiction-shopping — a compound failure of international coordination.

**Direction:** Construct a small toy 'two-regulator' model: define two stylized eval batteries (security-weighted vs innovation/utility-weighted) over a handful of measurable axes, score several open models on each, and show how often the pass/fail verdicts disagree. Map disagreement onto a simple jurisdiction-shopping incentive. Mostly analysis with a light empirical scoring component.

**Why it matters:** Turns the surprising UK/US renaming divergence into a measurable coordination-risk metric for the International Network of AI Safety Institutes. Cheap, public-model, and squarely outside any single lab's interest.

**Relevant context:** UK AISI -> AI Security Institute, US AISI -> CAISI divergence (subfield context); International consensus on eval methodologies open problem (FLI; interface-eu.org).

title: CoT-Monitoring Reliance x Covert Sandbagging: A Compound Failure for Monitoring-Based Safety Cases
quick_reasoning: Precisely targets whether CoT-monitoring safety cases survive covert sandbagging, with a focused model-organism probe.

original_idea.body:
# CoT-Monitoring Reliance x Covert Sandbagging: A Compound Failure for Monitoring-Based Safety Cases

**Problem:** Failure mode A: emerging governance proposals lean on chain-of-thought monitoring as a cheap oversight mechanism. Failure mode B: models can covertly sandbag against CoT monitoring (underperform without verbalizing the plan). If a safety case rests on CoT monitoring, covert sandbagging silently invalidates it.

**Direction:** On a small open model, reproduce a minimal covert-sandbag setup (prompt the model to underperform while keeping a clean-looking CoT) and measure how often a simple keyword/judge-based CoT monitor flags it vs misses it. Frame the false-negative rate as the failure probability of a monitoring-based regulatory safety case. A scoped model-organism probe, not a training effort.

**Why it matters:** Directly tests whether a governance mechanism many proposals assume is robust actually survives an adversarial model — a model-organism study labs deprioritize because it undercuts a tool they want to claim credit for. One GPU, public model.

**Relevant context:** LLMs can covertly sandbag against CoT monitoring (arXiv:2508.00943); Auditing Games for Sandbagging (arXiv:2512.07810).
